# OneCoin / “Cryptoqueen” Network: Publicly Documented Fraud Scheme and Enforcement Status

## Executive summary

The available evidence describes OneCoin as an international investment-fraud scheme presented as a cryptocurrency business. According to the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), OneCoin Ltd. began operating in 2014 from Sofia, Bulgaria, and marketed a cryptocurrency through a global multilevel-marketing (MLM) network. The DOJ states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide between 2014 and 2019 after being exposed to misrepresentations about the cryptocurrency’s value, blockchain, and transaction history. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The principal founders identified in the evidence are Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. The DOJ describes both as co-founders who, together with others, orchestrated the scheme. Separate legal commentary based on the prosecution record identifies Greenwood as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and states that he earned approximately 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, allegedly totaling more than $300 million. Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2023 and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The evidence supports a clear distinction between enforcement facts and unresolved matters. Greenwood’s sentence, the DOJ’s forfeiture activity, the establishment of a victim-remission process, and the availability of more than $40 million in forfeited assets are reported enforcement facts. By contrast, the exact present status and whereabouts of Ignatova remain unresolved in the supplied sources. The DOJ describes her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and says that the FBI continues efforts to locate her. The sources do not establish whether she is alive, dead, hiding, or otherwise unavailable; therefore, no conclusion about her physical status should be drawn from the supplied evidence.

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

Two sources were provided:

| Source ID | Source | Nature of source | Principal evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice press release dated April 13, 2026 | Official government announcement | Current remission process, scheme description, victim-loss estimate, forfeiture amount, agency roles, fugitive-status statement |
| S2 | ArentFox Schiff Investigations Blog article dated September 15, 2023 | Legal-industry secondary commentary | Greenwood’s sentence, alleged compensation and distributor role, representations attributed to prosecutors, historical enforcement context |

S1 is the more authoritative source for current U.S. government actions and the remission process. S2 is useful for contextualizing Greenwood’s sentence and alleged operational role but is secondary and should not displace the DOJ’s account where the two sources address the same matter.

## Reconstruction of the OneCoin scheme

### Origin, product, and operating period

The DOJ states that OneCoin began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. It marketed and sold a cryptocurrency called OneCoin through a global MLM network. The relevant fraud period identified by the DOJ is 2014 through 2019, and the remission process is directed to individuals who purchased OneCoin during that period. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The evidence therefore supports the following basic reconstruction:

1. OneCoin was organized as an international commercial and promotional operation.
2. Its product was presented as a cryptocurrency.
3. Distribution relied substantially on MLM recruitment and sales.
4. Investors were induced to buy OneCoin or related packages.
5. The scheme generated more than $4 billion in worldwide investment, according to the DOJ.

The supplied material does not establish the full corporate structure of OneCoin, the complete list of distributors, the identities of all alleged co-conspirators, or the precise geographic distribution of victims. Those matters should not be inferred from the two sources.

### Alleged technological misrepresentations

The legal-industry source reports that prosecutors alleged OneCoin made several material misrepresentations. These included claiming that OneCoin’s value was determined by market supply and demand, when prosecutors alleged that the value was instead set arbitrarily and without regard to market forces. Prosecutors also alleged that Greenwood represented OneCoin as having a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions, even though no publicly verifiable blockchain existed. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

These points should be characterized as prosecution allegations or factual assertions reported in legal commentary, rather than as independently established technical findings in the supplied materials. Nevertheless, they explain the central mechanism of the alleged fraud: investors were presented with a product represented as a functioning cryptocurrency whose value and transactional history had technological or market-based foundations that prosecutors said did not exist.

### MLM distribution and recruitment incentives

According to the DOJ, OneCoin was sold through a global MLM network. The legal-industry source adds that OneCoin members received commissions for recruiting other people to purchase cryptocurrency packages. Greenwood is described as the top MLM distributor, with an alleged entitlement to 5% of monthly OneCoin sales and alleged earnings exceeding $300 million. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

This structure is significant because it links the alleged fraud mechanism to recruitment. The supplied evidence does not merely describe passive sales of a digital asset; it describes a network in which participants were financially incentivized to recruit new purchasers. The available sources do not quantify the number of distributors, the percentage of revenue paid to different levels, or the total amount paid in commissions beyond the allegations concerning Greenwood.

## Principal founders and roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identifies Ruja Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin and states that she and Greenwood orchestrated the international investment scheme with others. The DOJ also describes Ignatova as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and states that the FBI continues to pursue information leading to her location. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The supplied sources establish her public association with the founding and operation of OneCoin. They do not provide a complete description of her specific management duties, financial role, technical responsibilities, or communications with investors. Accordingly, the supported role description is “co-founder and alleged organizer,” not a more detailed operational title.

The 2023 secondary source states that Ignatova “remains at large” and had been added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)) The later DOJ source continues to describe an active effort to locate her. These statements support the conclusion that her whereabouts were unresolved in the supplied record as of the DOJ’s April 2026 announcement.

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

The DOJ identifies Karl Sebastian Greenwood as a co-founder who, with Ignatova and others, orchestrated the scheme. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The secondary source provides more detail about Greenwood’s alleged role. It describes him as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and reports that prosecutors alleged he earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, amounting to more than $300 million. The source also reports that he was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The sentence is an enforcement outcome. The precise amount of Greenwood’s alleged earnings and his role in making particular representations should be described as prosecution allegations or reported allegations, even though he was sentenced.

## Enforcement actions and victim compensation

### Criminal prosecutions and forfeiture

The DOJ states that it filed multiple OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. It further states that several key figures were sentenced and that the government pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets were reported as available for victim compensation in the April 2026 announcement. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

Greenwood’s 20-year sentence is separately documented by S2, which also reports the approximately $300,000 forfeiture order. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

These figures should not be conflated. The $300,000 amount is reported as Greenwood’s individual forfeiture order, while the more than $40 million figure concerns forfeited assets available for the broader victim-compensation process. The supplied material does not explain the complete composition of the $40 million, whether it includes Greenwood’s forfeiture, or how the funds were allocated among particular defendants or assets.

### Remission process

The DOJ announced that victims who purchased OneCoin between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible to receive compensation through a remission process. The process is administered by Kroll Settlement Administration LLC, while the DOJ’s Criminal Division Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the compensation program. The DOJ identified June 30 as the petition deadline but did not specify the year in the supplied text. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The DOJ also stated that victims could obtain petition forms through the designated remission website or request forms from the Remission Administrator by telephone, email, or mail. It warned that neither the administrator nor the DOJ would charge a fee to participate. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The remission announcement is important for two reasons. First, it confirms that forfeiture proceedings produced assets intended for victim recovery. Second, it demonstrates that the government’s response was not limited to prosecution; it also included an administrative mechanism for processing victim claims.

## Enforcement facts versus unresolved claims

| Issue | Classification | Supported conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| OneCoin operated from 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria | Reported enforcement fact | Stated by the DOJ |
| More than $4 billion invested worldwide | Government-reported figure | DOJ identifies this as the scale of victim investment |
| OneCoin used an MLM network | Government-reported scheme description | Supported by S1 and S2 |
| Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years | Enforcement fact reported by S2 | Supported in the supplied record |
| Greenwood’s alleged earnings exceeded $300 million | Allegation reported by S2 | Should not be treated as an independently adjudicated amount |
| More than $40 million available for victim compensation | DOJ-reported enforcement fact | Supported by S1 |
| Ignatova was a co-founder | Government-reported fact | Supported by S1 |
| Ignatova’s current location | Unresolved | The sources do not establish it |
| Ignatova’s survival or death | Unresolved | No supplied source establishes either proposition |
| Ignatova remains a fugitive | Current enforcement characterization | DOJ says efforts to locate her continue |

The most important analytical conclusion is that “remains at large” or “fugitive” does not prove any particular theory about Ignatova’s whereabouts or physical condition. The evidence establishes an unresolved law-enforcement search, not the reason she has not been located.

## Assessment

On the supplied evidence, OneCoin is best characterized as a large-scale international investment-fraud scheme that used the language and commercial structure of cryptocurrency together with MLM recruitment incentives. The alleged deception operated at both the product level—through claims about value, blockchain functionality, and transaction records—and the distribution level—through commissions and recruitment.

Greenwood’s role is more concretely documented than Ignatova’s in the supplied record because the sources report his sentence, forfeiture order, and alleged position as the leading MLM distributor. Ignatova is clearly identified as a co-founder and alleged organizer, but the evidence supplied here does not provide enough detail to reconstruct her specific operational conduct beyond that description.

The enforcement record is materially developed: prosecutions were brought, Greenwood received a 20-year sentence, forfeiture was pursued, and a remission process was launched using more than $40 million in recovered assets. However, the record is incomplete regarding other defendants, the ultimate disposition of all prosecutions, the precise asset trail, the number of eligible victims, and the percentage of losses likely to be recovered.

## Conclusion

The public record supplied here supports a coherent reconstruction of OneCoin as a Bulgaria-based, internationally marketed cryptocurrency fraud that operated from 2014 through 2019 and obtained more than $4 billion from investors worldwide. Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood were the principal founders identified in the sources. Greenwood is associated with the scheme’s MLM distribution structure and has received a 20-year prison sentence. Ignatova remains the subject of an unresolved law-enforcement search.

The evidence does not justify claims that Ignatova is dead, secretly detained, definitively living under another identity, or located in any particular country. The defensible conclusion is narrower: she was identified by the DOJ as a co-founder and FBI Top Ten Fugitive, and her current whereabouts and physical status remain unresolved in the supplied sources.

## References

ArentFox Schiff. (2023, September 15). *Co-founder of fraudulent cryptocurrency sentenced to 20 years in prison*. Investigations Blog. [https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs. (2026, April 13). *Justice Department announces compensation process for OneCoin fraud victims with funds recovered through asset forfeiture*. [https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)
